analysis.one_liner: Lets insurers keep selling pre-ACA group health plans outside the new exchanges through 2016.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no cosponsors and never came to a vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let health insurance companies keep offering, for new sale, the kind of group health plans they sold during 2013 — plans that do not meet the Affordable Care Act's coverage rules — through the end of 2016, outside the ACA's health insurance exchanges. It would treat those plans as "grandfathered," meaning people covered by them would count as having the required health coverage. The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: Insurance companies that wanted to keep selling cheaper, less-regulated group plans alongside ACA-compliant products, and the employers and workers who preferred those older plans because they cost less. The trade-off is that those plans could skimp on coverage the ACA requires, and every healthier group that stayed out of the ACA-compliant pool left the exchanges with a sicker, more expensive mix of customers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurers and employers wanting cheaper plans

how_it_helps.text: Any insurer that sold group coverage at any point in 2013 could keep selling that same coverage through 2016 outside the ACA exchanges, rather than being pushed into the exchange market.
Coverage sold under this carve-out would count as a grandfathered plan for the individual mandate, so people holding it would not face a penalty for lacking ACA-compliant coverage.
Employers and workers who preferred their pre-ACA plans — often cheaper because they covered less — would have had a legal path to keep buying them for two more years.

analysis.who_pays: People who remain in ACA-compliant plans, especially exchange customers: if healthier groups keep buying older, skinnier plans instead, the compliant risk pool gets sicker and premiums rise for everyone left in it. Buyers of the grandfathered plans also give up ACA protections such as essential health benefits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Exchange customers left in ACA plans

drawbacks.text: Plans sold under this exception would not have to meet the ACA's coverage rules, so buyers could hold policies that skimp on essential benefits and coverage protections.

Every employer or group that chose a cheaper non-compliant plan instead of ACA-compliant coverage would pull healthier members out of the compliant pool, raising premiums for the people who stayed — including exchange customers.
The two-year window would have ended in 2016, giving employers and insurers a temporary patch rather than a stable long-term rule and setting up another disruption when it expired.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a modest, temporary benefit — two more years of cheaper but weaker group plans for some employers and workers — against a real cost: it would have let healthier, cheaper-to-cover groups keep buying plans outside the ACA's rules, leaving a sicker pool behind and pushing premiums up for exchange customers. It was also a very narrow bill that touched only the group market and only through 2016, so its effects would have been limited either way. As a policy design, it addressed a real complaint about canceled plans but did so by opening a hole in the coverage standards rather than strengthening the transition.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bruce Braley introduced the bill on September 11, 2014, about three weeks before the end of the session's work period and one month before the November 2014 elections.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and the next day the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health received the health-related portions.
No further action was taken: no cosponsors signed on, no committee reported the bill, and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, no new carve-out from the ACA's coverage rules was created, so exchange customers and the ACA-compliant risk pool were spared further siphoning of healthier groups. Insurers and employers hoping for the exception did not get it, though the change was small and the existing transitional rules continued regardless.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: ACA exchange risk pools; status quo held

sides.party_line_note: A single House Democrat sponsored the bill and not one member of either party cosponsored it, so it never drew a partisan test on the floor or in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have let insurers keep selling pre-ACA group plans — cheaper to buy, less regulated, fewer required benefits — as a separate product line through 2016. Their interest partly aligned with buyers who wanted lower premiums, but the exception would also have weakened the ACA-compliant market those same insurers sell into.

Employers could have kept buying cheaper pre-ACA plans for two more years, lowering their benefit costs. Workers on those plans paid less but gave up ACA-required benefits, and the shift raised costs for people left in compliant coverage.
